title: Things Left Behind
connection_reasons: Three lyrics about the same aftermath: things a person left behind that cannot be moved yet (the grey sweater, the toothbrush) and the question of whether any of it was real.
All three share the same longing and the same refusal to say the ending out loud.

next_action.action: Write a chorus that says plainly what the sweater and the toothbrush are avoiding, and try ending it on 'and called it love'.

fragments.title: The Grey Sweater
fragments.text:
still got your sweater the grey one
I wore it to the grocery store Tuesday
some lady asked if I was okay
I said yeah I'm fine just cold but it's August
fragments.raw_text:
still got your sweater the grey one
I wore it to the grocery store Tuesday
some lady asked if I was okay
I said yeah I'm fine just cold but it's August
fragments.suggestion: The details do the work: a grey sweater, a grocery store on a Tuesday, a stranger asking if you are okay. 'But it's August' is the turn; the excuse falls apart inside the line, and the word heartbreak never has to appear. Keep the delivery close to spoken. What is missing is a chorus that steps back from the objects and says the feeling plainly, once.

fragments.agent_narrative: The sweater is the first thing left behind in this set. I put it with the toothbrush and the front row ticket: all three are about an ending nobody says out loud.

fragments.title: Three Weeks
fragments.text:
it's been three weeks now
and your toothbrush is still here
I should probably move it
but then it's really real
fragments.raw_text:
it's been three weeks now
and your toothbrush is still here
I should probably move it
but then it's really real
fragments.suggestion: Four plain lines hold a whole situation: three weeks, a toothbrush, and the reason it stays. 'But then it's really real' is the line everything leans on, so give it the longest note. The understatement is the strength; do not add an explanation after it. This could open a verse that a later chorus answers.
fragments.connection_reason: Three lyrics about the same aftermath: things a person left behind that cannot be moved yet (the grey sweater, the toothbrush) and the question of whether any of it was real.
fragments.agent_narrative: Like the sweater, the toothbrush stays because moving it would make the ending real. I grouped it with the other two lyrics about the same aftermath.

fragments.title: Front Row Ticket
fragments.text:
was any of it real or just mirrors
maybe it was always a show
and I just bought a front row ticket
and called it love
fragments.raw_text:
was any of it real or just mirrors
maybe it was always a show
and I just bought a front row ticket
and called it love
fragments.suggestion: This states a whole idea in four lines and ends on the phrase worth remembering, which is what a chorus needs. The mirror image runs into the theatre image, the show and the front row ticket, and 'and called it love' closes it. Try the first line close to a whisper and let the voice open up by the last. Leave a beat of silence after 'called it love'.

fragments.agent_narrative: This asks the question the other two lines circle around, whether any of it was real. It reads like the chorus for the sweater and toothbrush verses.
